findings.paper_title: SOUTH for briefing Cabinet scene setting report Oct 2026
findings.headline: £3.0 million provision set aside in reserves for LGR implementation costs, allocation still to be determined.
findings.detail: The council has set aside £3.0 million in reserves specifically for the transitional costs of implementing Local Government Reorganisation. Work continues to identify how these funds will be allocated. With LGR now paused, the need for and timing of these costs is uncertain.
findings.matters: Represents a material contingency (roughly 15 per cent of annual revenue income) that depends on an uncertain event and could be redeployed if LGR is delayed or cancelled.
findings.figures: £3.0 million
findings.quote: A provision of £3.0 million has been set aside in reserves and work continues to identify how these funds will be allocated

findings.paper_title: SOUTH for briefing Cabinet scene setting report Oct 2026
findings.headline: Managed vacancy factor target of £250,000 cannot be achieved due to high staff retention.
findings.detail: The council set a reduced managed vacancy factor target of £250,000 for budget purposes but has been unable to achieve it because of high levels of staff retention. The council will review this position further, but the assumed headcount reduction is not delivering.
findings.matters: Shows the council cannot achieve planned staffing reductions, constraining its options for cost management.
findings.figures: £250,000 target
findings.quote: the managed vacancy factor was reduced to £250,000, but we are still seeing a high level of staff retention which means the council has been unable to meet this level and therefore it will be reviewed further.

findings.paper_title: SOUTH for briefing Cabinet scene setting report Oct 2026
findings.headline: Pay award for 2026/27 expected to be 3.8 per cent, up from the anticipated 3 per cent.
findings.detail: The budget for 2026/27 was set on a pay award assumption of 3 per cent. This is now expected to be 3.8 per cent, though the outcome remains subject to ongoing negotiation with UNISON. This represents an emerging cost pressure not reflected in the adopted budget.
findings.matters: Signals an unexpected cost pressure emerging mid-year and likely affecting peers, creating budget risk if the 3.8 per cent outcome is locked in.
findings.figures: 3 per cent assumed, 3.8 per cent expected
findings.quote: the pay award for 2026/27 was anticipated to be three per cent, as per the pay agreement this is now expected to be 3.8 per cent but is subject to negotiation with UNISON.

findings.paper_title: SOUTH for briefing Cabinet scene setting report Oct 2026
findings.headline: Interest rate changes of 1 per cent could shift investment income by more than £1 million annually.
findings.detail: The council explicitly flags that interest rate volatility creates significant income risk, noting that rates are continuing to remain higher than expected. It illustrates the risk with a specific figure: a one per cent change in the average interest rate on investments could result in more than a £1 million change in investment income over a year.
findings.matters: Shows the council's investment income forecast is sensitive to macro-economic factors, with material downside risk if rates fall.
findings.figures: £1 million per 1 per cent change in average interest rate
findings.quote: interest rates are continuing to remain higher than expected and by way of illustration, a one per cent change in the average interest rate on investments could result in more than a £1 million change in investment income over a year.

findings.paper_title: SOUTH for briefing Cabinet scene setting report Oct 2026
findings.headline: Reserve usage projected at £4,632k in 2030/31 against £3,765k threshold, with headroom shrinking from £4,373k in 2027/28 to £485k in 2029/30
findings.detail: The February 2026 MTFP showed sustainable reserve usage in the first four years, but from 2030/31 onwards 'increasingly unsustainable' use of reserves will be required to balance the budget. By 2030/31, estimated reserve usage exceeds the 10 per cent threshold by £867k. The path to that point shows headroom shrinking from £4,373k in 2027/28 to £485k in 2029/30.
findings.matters: Shows a structural budget problem requiring action if the council exists beyond 2030/31, a key concern for peers and lenders assessing medium-term solvency.
findings.figures: 2027/28: £141k use against £4,232k threshold (£4,373k headroom); 2028/29: £1,394k use against £4,096k threshold (£2,702k headroom); 2029/30: £3,422k use against £3,907k threshold (£485k headroom); 2030/31: £4,632k use against £3,765k threshold (£867k gap)
findings.quote: from 2030/31 onwards, the use of reserves was increasingly unsustainable and required action by the council to address the increasing budget gap

findings.paper_title: SOUTH for briefing Cabinet scene setting report Oct 2026
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation paused on 7 September 2026, leaving unclear when or if this council will be replaced.
findings.detail: Government had announced a minded-to decision in July 2026 for unitary councils from 1 April 2028. On 7 September 2026 the government paused the LGR process. The council now assumes it is most likely to exist in 2028/29 and set a budget for that year, but the vesting day could still be 1 April 2028 or later than 1 April 2029.
findings.matters: Finance directors and lenders need to understand if and when the council will exist, and how that affects debt servicing and planning horizons.
findings.figures: 7 September 2026 pause date, original vesting date 1 April 2028, possible vesting date 1 April 2029 or later
findings.quote: However, on Monday 7 September 2026 the government announced that the LGR process has been paused, meaning that – as it stands – the minded-to decision is being reviewed. It is now not clear what new council or councils will replace this council, and when that will take place.

findings.headline: Investment returns remained robust despite falling interest rates, with councils operating within approved treasury management strategies throughout the year.
findings.detail: Despite a declining interest rate environment, both councils maintained effective investment management and governance compliance. The councils continued to invest with regard for security, liquidity and yield in that order, and received prior scrutiny of all treasury management reports from the Joint Audit and Governance Committee before reporting to Full Council.
findings.matters: Consistent delivery of treasury management objectives despite economic headwinds, combined with full governance compliance and regular member scrutiny, demonstrates sound financial stewardship.
findings.figures: Investment returns remained robust during period of three 0.25 per cent base rate cuts. All councils operated within treasury limits and Prudential Indicators.
findings.quote: During the financial year, the councils operated within the treasury limits and Prudential Indicators set out in their Treasury Management Strategies approved by Council in February 2025.

findings.headline: Neither council required borrowing during 2025-26 and both maintained prudent debt management within approved treasury strategy limits.
findings.detail: Both South Oxfordshire and Vale of White Horse operated throughout the year without any need to borrow. The councils maintained their treasury management approach within the limits and prudential indicators set in their Treasury Management Strategies, which were approved by Council in February 2025.
findings.matters: Avoiding new borrowing despite ongoing service pressures demonstrates effective cash management and reduces refinancing risk and exposure to market rate movements.
findings.figures: Zero borrowing during 2025-26 financial year. Prudential indicators met and within approved limits.
findings.quote: During 2025/26, there has not been a need for either council to borrow and both councils continue to take a prudent approach to their debt strategy.

findings.paper_title: Appendix E - Treasury Invest as at 31 March 2026
findings.headline: South Oxfordshire holds £11.7m in L&G Equities Unit Trust—7% of its treasury portfolio—while Vale of White Horse holds no equities
findings.detail: South Oxfordshire's £165.1m treasury portfolio includes £11,731,634 in L&G Equities Unit Trust at variable rate. Vale of White Horse's £158.7m portfolio contains no equity holdings, investing instead in fixed-rate council deposits, building society deposits, and property and money market funds. Equities subject to market volatility are atypical in local authority treasury functions, which typically prioritise capital preservation and liquidity.
findings.matters: A lender would want to understand the treasury strategy and risk posture; equity holdings signal either a reserve component managed through treasury or tolerance for market risk within the treasury function—unusual for councils and material to financial resilience assessment.
findings.figures: South Oxfordshire: £11,731,634 (7% of £165,094,226); Vale of White Horse: £0 in equities
findings.quote: L&G Equities Unit Trust   11,731,634  variable

findings.paper_title: Appendix E - Treasury Invest as at 31 March 2026
findings.headline: Both councils hold substantial fixed-rate investments in Central Bedfordshire, Cornwall, and Devon & Cornwall Police at 6.4–8.0%, with maturities in April 2026
findings.detail: South Oxfordshire has invested £14m in Central Bedfordshire (£5m at 7.0%), Cornwall (£6m at 7.5%), and PCC Devon & Cornwall (£3m at 8.0%), all maturing 23–30 April 2026. Vale of White Horse has £13m invested similarly, maturing 16–27 April. These rates are 2.5–3.5 percentage points above the 4.1–4.65% earned on other local authority deposits in the same portfolios and substantially above current market rates for short-term council paper.
findings.matters: A lender would want to understand why both councils achieved such high short-term rates for local authority investments; this may reflect credit concerns at the borrowing councils or represent exceptional pricing that warrants explanation.

findings.headline: Treasury team implemented operational improvements including ICD investment platform yielding 0.2 per cent return improvement
findings.detail: Treasury staff demonstrated continued proactive improvement throughout 2025-26, including daily late-afternoon balance reviews, intensive cash management during Christmas holiday period (investing £33 million for two councils over this period), and in February adopting ICD investment platform allowing daily selection from multiple money market funds. Early indications suggest platform change generated 0.2 per cent income improvement.
findings.matters: Shows active treasury management discipline and operational excellence with measurable yield improvements from process and platform enhancements.
findings.figures: 0.2% income improvement from ICD platform; £33 million invested during Christmas period
findings.quote: In February the councils moved to using 'ICD', an investment platform which allows the choice from a number of money market funds each day. Early indications suggest using this platform has led to an increase in money market income of 0.2 per cent.

findings.headline: Average rate of return on deposits declined to 4.82 per cent from 4.95 per cent
findings.detail: Despite outperforming benchmarks and peer group, average rate of return on internally managed treasury deposits fell from 4.95 per cent in 2024-25 to 4.82 per cent in 2025-26, indicating interest rate environment moved lower through the year even while remaining 0.88 per cent above 3-month SONIA benchmark.
findings.matters: Signals shifting interest rate environment and indicates lower investment returns likely for future years, affecting treasury income planning.
findings.quote: The actual average rate of return on internally managed treasury deposits for the year was 4.82 per cent (4.95 per cent in 2024/25).

findings.headline: Council outperformed MUFG benchmarking group average by 0.23 per cent
findings.detail: In MUFG Benchmarking Club peer comparison, council achieved 0.23 per cent above peer average return while maintaining very low risk profile with investments concentrated in local authorities and money market funds. This reflects consistent strong treasury management execution.
findings.matters: Peer outperformance with low-risk profile demonstrates above-average treasury management capability and effective risk management discipline.
findings.figures: 0.23% above peer group average; average deposit return 4.82% versus benchmark 3.94%
findings.quote: The council outperformed the average of the group by 0.23 per cent with a very low risk profile of investments, mainly with local authorities and money market funds.

findings.headline: Investment property portfolio swung from £0.681 million loss to £0.963 million income
findings.detail: Council's portfolio of investment properties (land, depots, garages, shops let on commercial basis) generated £0.963 million income in 2025-26 versus £0.681 million loss in prior year, representing £1.644 million positive swing. Portfolio achieved 17.6 per cent gross return. Net book value of portfolio £5.7 million at 31 March 2026, up from £5.1 million prior year.
findings.matters: Shows significant improvement in property asset performance and demonstrates changed contribution to council income; portfolio now generating material returns.
findings.figures: £0.963m income (2025-26), £0.681m loss (2024-25), 17.6% gross return, £5.7m net book value (up from £5.1m)
findings.quote: Income generated was £0.963 million in 2025/26 (£0.681 million loss in 2024/25) giving a gross rate of return of 17.6 per cent.

findings.headline: New office development removed from capital programme affecting cash deployment
findings.detail: Council's capital programme was modified during 2025-26, with new office development removed. This change contributed to higher cash balances than forecast, which in turn enabled higher investment returns. The timing of capital spend was also rephased during the year.
findings.matters: Capital programme changes signal revised priorities or scope; affects financial planning, cash deployment strategy, and borrowing requirements.
findings.figures: Not quantified; cited as primary reason for variance between forecast and actual cash balances
findings.quote: Cash balances were also higher than forecast in the budget, primarily due to the phasing of capital spend and the removal of the new office development from the programme.

findings.headline: Investment income £1.25 million above budget at £8.6 million
findings.detail: Council earned £8.6 million on investments versus £7.3 million budget. Outperformance driven by deposits earning £1.1 million more than forecast due to sustained higher interest rates, higher cash balances from capital spend phasing and removal of new office development from programme, and treasury team operational improvements including adoption of ICD investment platform yielding 0.2 per cent return improvement.
findings.matters: Demonstrates better treasury management execution and indicates either stronger cash position or more effective rate management than anticipated in budget.
findings.figures: £8.6m actual, £7.3m budget, £1.25m outperformance; deposits £1.1m higher; 0.2% yield improvement from platform change
findings.quote: The total income earned on investments during 2025/26 was £8.6 million, compared to the original budget of £7.3 million

findings.headline: 2024/25 internal audit concluded satisfactory control environment; 2025/26 audits achieved 3 limited assurance ratings from 22 reviews
findings.detail: The internal audit and risk manager's 2024/25 annual report concluded "a satisfactory system of governance, risk, internal control" with "some enhancements have been recommended." In 2025/26, the committee reviewed quarterly progress reports covering 22 audit reviews, of which "only three limited assurance ratings" were recorded, indicating consistent strong control performance.
findings.matters: A satisfactory audit opinion demonstrates management controls are effective; consistent strong results reassure stakeholders and lenders about governance quality
findings.figures: 22 audits reviewed in 2025/26; 3 limited assurance ratings; satisfactory opinion in 2024/25
findings.quote: Internal audit assurance: Monitored delivery of the 2025/26 internal audit plan, reviewed findings from 22 audits (with only three limited assurance ratings).

findings.headline: Overdue internal audit recommendations backlog described as excessive; committee reports numbers now reducing
findings.detail: External auditors noted the number of overdue internal audit recommendations as a matter arising from the 2024/25 audit. The committee told officers "the number of overdue recommendations was excessive" and pressed for reduction. Recent reports show improvement, though the committee has indicated it will "continue to hold officers to account on this matter." The committee continues to receive regular updates on overdue Priority 1 actions.
findings.matters: Overdue audit recommendations signal delayed management response to control findings; a finance director or lender would want to see whether the council is managing audit follow-up effectively
findings.figures: No specific backlog numbers provided; trajectory shows improvement
findings.quote: The committee made it clear that the number of overdue recommendations was excessive, and through officers expressed the need for them to be reduced. Recent reports have demonstrated that the numbers are reducing but the committee will continue to hold officers to account on this matter.

findings.headline: 2024/25 accounts disclaimed; auditors' roadmap targets 2026/27 for unqualified accounts
findings.detail: The audit of the 2024/25 accounts was concluded in February 2026. The accounts were disclaimed by Bishop Fleming "in common with those of a significant number of councils nationwide as a result of the well documented issues within local audit." The auditors have provided a roadmap for returning to unqualified accounts, with the aim that 2025/26 accounts are qualified and 2026/27 accounts become unqualified, subject to progress with their "build back" activity.
findings.matters: Finance directors and lenders need to understand audit risk: whether the council can achieve qualified accounts and when, and what obstacles remain
findings.figures: Accounts published February 2026; aim for 2025/26 qualified, 2026/27 unqualified
findings.quote: The auditors discussed their intended roadmap for returning to unqualified accounts for both councils, with the aim being that the 2025/26 accounts are qualified, and the 2026/27 accounts being unqualified. This is subject to satisfactory progress with their "build back" activity.

findings.headline: Investment property income fell to £0.19 million from £0.22 million; asset values declined from £3.97 million to £3.44 million
findings.detail: The council's commercial property holdings generated lower rental income in 2025-26 and declined in book value by £0.53 million year-on-year. While the paper notes that whole-life costs are excluded from these valuations, the simultaneous decline in both income and capital value signals a weakening contribution from this asset class.
findings.matters: Declining rental income and capital values from investment properties warrant monitoring as they reduce total investment returns and may signal weakness in the commercial property market segments where the council holds assets.
findings.figures: Income £0.19 million (2025-26) vs £0.22 million (2024-25); net book value £3.44 million vs £3.97 million; gross return on property 5.4%
findings.quote: These assets are valued on an annual basis and had an average net book value of £3.44 million at 31 March 2026 (£3.97 million as at 31 March 2025). Income generated was £0.19 million (£0.22 million in 2025/26).

findings.headline: Treasury investments outperformed all benchmarks: bank deposits 0.36% above benchmark, CCLA fund 0.34% above, peer group average by 0.40 basis points
findings.detail: The council achieved a 4.30% return on bank and building society deposits against a 3.94% benchmark, and 4.35% on its CCLA property fund against a 4.01% benchmark. Performance against the MUFG Benchmarking club peer group was strong while maintaining a low-risk investment profile concentrated in local authorities and money market funds.
findings.matters: Consistent outperformance of treasury benchmarks indicates strong asset management capability and effective deployment of idle cash, particularly valuable when achieved within a conservative risk profile.
findings.figures: Bank deposits 4.30% actual vs 3.94% benchmark (0.36% outperformance); CCLA 4.35% actual vs 4.01% benchmark (0.34% outperformance)
findings.quote: The council outperformed the average of the group by 0.40 basis points with a very low risk profile of investments, mainly with local authorities and money market funds.

findings.headline: Investment interest earned £8.1 million, £2.1 million above budget of £4.3 million
findings.detail: The council's treasury investments delivered significantly higher returns than forecast, primarily because of sustained higher interest rates throughout the year and higher cash balances than anticipated. This outperformance directly improves the council's cash position and reduces dependency on external borrowing.
findings.matters: A council that generates higher-than-expected investment income improves its financial flexibility and capacity to fund reserves, capital projects, or service pressures without additional borrowing.
findings.figures: Actual interest £8.1 million vs budget £4.3 million; outperformance £2.1 million; average rate of return 4.30%
findings.quote: The total interest earned on treasury investments during 2025/26 was £8.1 million compared to the original budget estimate of £4.3m million

findings.headline: Both councils remained within all treasury limits and prudential indicators set for the year.
findings.detail: South Oxfordshire and Vale of White Horse operated their treasury function entirely within the parameters approved by Full Council in February 2025. All prudential indicators and treasury limits were observed throughout the financial year and at outturn.
findings.matters: Treasury limits and prudential indicators control risk and prevent excessive exposure to interest rate or counterparty movements; compliance demonstrates effective governance and that the risk framework is proportionate and applied.
findings.figures: All prudential indicators and limits complied with throughout 2025-26
findings.quote: During the financial year, the councils operated within the treasury limits and Prudential Indicators set out in their Treasury Management Strategies approved by Council in February 2025.

findings.headline: Neither South Oxfordshire nor Vale of White Horse required borrowing during 2025-26.
findings.detail: Both councils had sufficient cash balances and investment income to cover outgoings without accessing the borrowing market. Both councils continue to take a prudent approach to debt strategy. Prudential indicators and limits provide scope to borrow in the short term if future cash flow needs arise.
findings.matters: Absence of borrowing requirement indicates strong cash generation and reserves; unexpected borrowing signals financial stress; strong reserves reduce risk to lenders and borrowing costs if borrowing becomes necessary.
findings.figures: No borrowing in 2025-26
findings.quote: During 2025/26, there has not been a need for either council to borrow and both councils continue to take a prudent approach to their debt strategy.

findings.headline: Base Rate fell more slowly than the Treasury Management Strategy had forecast, enabling councils to place deposits at above-budgeted rates.
findings.detail: The 2025-26 Treasury Management Strategy forecast that Bank Base Rate would reach 3.75% by Q1 2025-26. In practice, the Monetary Policy Committee made three 0.25% cuts during the year (May, August, December 2025), reaching 3.75% in March 2026. This slower reduction path than anticipated allowed the councils to place temporary cash balances at interest rates above budgeted assumptions.
findings.matters: Interest rate forecasting determines investment income budgets; councils that forecast conservatively on rate cuts benefit when cuts arrive more slowly than expected; the pace and scale of rate movements affects the MTFP.
findings.figures: Base Rate 4.5% at year start, 3.75% at year end; three cuts of 0.25% each in May, August, December 2025
findings.quote: The slower cuts in the Base Rate than originally forecast, allowed both councils to place deposits at above budgeted interest rates and generate investment returns above the budget forecasts.

findings.headline: South Oxfordshire generated £8.6m treasury investment income and Vale of White Horse £6.4m, both exceeding budgets.
findings.detail: South Oxfordshire's treasury investments generated £8.6m actual income and Vale of White Horse achieved £6.4m, both exceeding budgeted forecasts. Total investment income across both councils (including property and non-treasury loans) was £9.5m for Vale and £6.6m for South. The outperformance resulted from interest rate cuts in the economy being slower than the councils' strategy had forecast, allowing deposits to earn above-budgeted rates.
findings.matters: Investment income is material to both councils' medium-term financial plans and contributes directly to reserves or supports service expenditure; forecast accuracy in this area affects financial sustainability and planning reliability.
findings.figures: South treasury investment income £8.6m actual, Vale £6.4m actual; both exceeded budgeted forecasts
findings.quote: Both South and Vale exceeded treasury budgeted investment income this year in terms of actual income.

findings.headline: New lone working system (People Safe) implemented August 2026; embedding into reviews recommended
findings.detail: LoneAlert was replaced by People Safe in August 2026. The audit recommends the team leader embed a review of system usage into regular employee review processes, as the system is relatively new. Training remains ongoing.
findings.matters: Proper embedding and oversight of new systems supports employee safety and ensures controls operate effectively as intended.
findings.figures: Implementation date August 2026
findings.quote: In August 2026, LoneAlert was replaced by People Safe: as the system is relatively new, we recommend the team leader embeds a review of system usage into the regular employee review process.

findings.headline: Officer impersonation fraud attempt identified locally; no financial loss incurred
findings.detail: One local incident of attempted officer impersonation occurred during the review period. The licensee contacted the council to verify the request and identified it as fraudulent, preventing loss. Testing confirmed that premises licence renewals are processed through invoices sent to registered addresses, reducing fraud risk.
findings.matters: Officer impersonation affects council revenue collection, reputational risk, and licence holder confidence. Mitigation through process design (official invoices to registered addresses) reduces exposure.
findings.figures: One local incident during review period
findings.quote: One local incident was identified during the review period; however, no financial loss was incurred as the licensee contacted the Council to verify the request and established that it was fraudulent.

findings.headline: Licensing procedures lack documented review dates; enforcement procedures not reviewed since December 2020
findings.detail: Of 39 procedures reviewed, enforcement and other procedures had not been reviewed since December 2020. No evidence of documented review dates or planned next review dates exists across all 39 procedures, although the licensing team confirmed a two-year review cycle is intended.
findings.matters: Outdated or non-compliant procedures could lead to legal exposure and non-compliance with licensing legislation. Formal documentation of review cycles supports compliance and continuity.
findings.figures: 39 procedures total; some not reviewed since December 2020
findings.quote: Some procedures had not been reviewed since December 2020... For all 39 procedures reviewed, there was no evidence of documented review dates or planned next review dates.

findings.headline: Testing identified insufficient evidence of compliance with statutory advertising requirements for licence changes
findings.detail: While key controls for licence applications and renewals were generally operating effectively, testing found exceptions where controls were not operating as intended, specifically insufficient documentation of statutory advertising compliance when licence changes occurred.
findings.matters: Failure to comply with statutory advertising requirements could invalidate licensing decisions and create legal exposure for the council.
findings.figures: A few exceptions identified in control testing
findings.quote: However, a few exceptions were identified where controls were not operating as intended, including insufficient evidence of compliance with statutory advertising requirements for licence changes.

findings.headline: Licensing income controls operating effectively; all fees charged correctly against 2025-26 schedule
findings.detail: Testing of sampled premises licence invoices confirmed they were correctly prepared, requisitioned and approved. Fees charged were agreed to the Licensing and Community Safety Fees 2025-26 with no discrepancies identified. The monthly renewal process uses a master spreadsheet reconciled against the Uniform licensing management system.
findings.matters: Reliable collection and recording of licensing income supports council cash flow and revenue forecasting; effective controls reduce the risk of lost revenue.
findings.figures: No discrepancies identified in fee testing
findings.quote: For all licence types, the amounts charged were agreed to the Licensing and Community Safety Fees 2025-26. No discrepancies were identified.

findings.headline: Licensing audit assurance upgraded from satisfactory to substantial since 2017
findings.detail: The 2026/27 audit found substantial assurance in governance, risk management and control. This is an improvement from the previous audit in May 2017, which gave satisfactory assurance. The audit identified 4 priority 3 actions but no priority 1 or 2 findings.
findings.matters: An upgrade in audit assurance for a council service demonstrates enhanced internal controls and governance, improving the overall audit opinion and control environment.
findings.figures: Last audited May 2017 (Satisfactory assurance); current finding Substantial with 4 priority 3 actions
findings.quote: Substantial A sound system of governance, risk management and control exists, with internal controls operating effectively and being consistently applied to support the achievement of objectives in the area audited.

findings.matters: Cyber security and data protection are fundamental operational and financial risks; Limited assurance indicates the council faces material control weaknesses in systems and data security.

findings.headline: Audit finds specialist sign-offs missing from financial and legal implications review in Cabinet reports
findings.detail: The internal audit gave a Substantial assurance opinion on the report lifecycle process but identified control gaps. In a sample of 20 reports submitted to Cabinet and committees since January 2026, five checklists lacked sign-off from specialist officers confirming they had reviewed the financial, legal, and risk implications. The audit flagged as a key risk that this could result in inaccurate or incomplete information reaching Cabinet. Additionally, four service areas did not use the approved report templates.
findings.matters: Cabinet financial decisions depend on accurate information about implications; specialist review sign-offs ensure that financial and legal considerations have been properly evaluated before decision-makers receive reports.
findings.figures: 5 checklists missing specialist officer sign-off on implications (out of 20 sampled); 4 of 20 reports did not use approved templates; 2 Priority 2 actions identified
findings.quote: Five checklists (one South and four Vale) did not include signoff from the relevant specialist officer to evidence consultation on the implication sections.

findings.headline: South Oxfordshire and Vale of White Horse councils took no external borrowing in 2025-26 despite prudential budgets allowing for up to £35m
findings.detail: Original prudential limits authorized borrowing of £30-35m for South Oxfordshire and £25-30m operational boundary, with planned headroom for up to £10m in other long-term liabilities. Actual external borrowing and long-term liabilities were zero for both councils at 31 March 2026, indicating capital and operational needs were met from internal resources without accessing capital markets.
findings.matters: Councils that don't need to borrow despite planning for significant amounts demonstrate strong reserve position and absence of funding pressure—material to lenders assessing credit risk and to other councils evaluating reserve adequacy and capital planning

findings.headline: 67 of 131 open audit actions are past their implementation deadline, representing 51 per cent of all outstanding findings
findings.detail: As of 25 September 2026, the council holds 131 open audit management actions (16 Priority 1, 83 Priority 2, 32 Priority 3), of which 67 are overdue against their management-committed completion dates. This high proportion of overdue actions suggests systematic difficulty in implementing audit remedies within planned timescales. The backlog includes actions across multiple audit years, though 96 (73 per cent) of the 131 open actions were raised during 2025/26 and 2026/27, indicating that recent audit findings are also experiencing implementation delays.
findings.matters: A high proportion of overdue audit actions indicates weak management follow-through on control improvements, suggests escalating risk exposure, and signals that internal control deficiencies identified by audit are not being remediated at pace.
findings.figures: 67 past due out of 131 open actions (51%); 96 actions (73%) raised in 2025/26–2026/27
findings.quote: Of these 131 actions, 67 are past due. Since the last update, we raised 65 new actions, 105 actions were closed, and 51 actions are implemented, awaiting evidence or validation by internal audit.

findings.headline: Eight Priority 1 audit actions remain overdue as of 25 September 2026, with greatest concentration in property site visit audits
findings.detail: Eight Priority 1 management actions (defined as fundamental to business process integrity requiring immediate attention) are past their implementation deadlines. These concentrate in Development & Corporate Landlord property audits: Abbey House (3 actions), Cornerstone (2 actions) and Beacon (1 action), plus one further Cornerstone site visit action. Management has not delivered these fundamental controls within agreed timescales.
findings.matters: Priority 1 actions address control gaps fundamental to business integrity; their persistent overdue status suggests either insufficient management capacity to remediate, or deprioritization of critical weaknesses, and indicates broader control environment frailty.
findings.figures: 8 Priority 1 actions overdue out of 16 Priority 1 actions total (50%)
findings.quote: the 8 past due, priority 1 actions as of 25th September 2026, relate to the following audits: Site Visit (Abbey House) 25/26 3; Site Visit (Cornerstone) 2; Site Visit (Beacon) 1; Site Visit (Cornerstone) 1

findings.headline: Cyber Security audit for 2025/26 rated Limited assurance with nine management actions including two Priority 1 findings
findings.detail: The cyber security audit (including AI) completed in 2025/26 was rated Limited assurance, indicating significant gaps and weaknesses in controls. Limited assurance means significant gaps, weaknesses or non-compliance were identified requiring improvement to manage risks effectively. The audit generated nine management actions: two Priority 1 (fundamental to service integrity) and five Priority 2 (important findings).
findings.matters: Cyber security is a material control area; a Limited rating indicates the council faces significant information security or data protection gaps that could affect financial systems, operational resilience, and compliance.
findings.figures: 2 Priority 1 actions, 5 Priority 2 actions, 9 total actions from cyber security audit
findings.quote: Cyber Security (incl. AI) 25/26 Limited 9 2 5 2

findings.headline: Disabled facilities grant underspend of £1.1m being reviewed by Department of Health and Social Care
findings.detail: Council forecasts £1.1m underspend on disabled facilities grant for the year based on Q1 run rate. The Department for Health and Social Care is currently reviewing DFG underspends nationally. Underspend will be profiled into future years.
findings.matters: Central government scrutiny of DFG underspends signals potential policy risk; material capital budget underspend could indicate procurement capacity constraints or demand assumptions that do not hold
findings.figures: £1.1m underspend predicted on disabled facilities grant; approved capital programme £43.632m with £3.638m spent (8%) by end June
findings.quote: Disabled facilities grant is underspent and whilst spend will continue through the year, a £1.1 million underspend against budget is predicted for this year based on the first quarter spend.  This underspend will be profiled into future years.  The Department for Health and Social Care are currently reviewing DFG underspends.

findings.headline: Planning service lacks in-house capability, paying external consultants for planning appeals
findings.detail: Planning department is forecasting an overspend because it does not have the expertise to conduct planning appeals work in house and must engage external consultants instead.
findings.matters: Inability to resource core functions internally and reliance on expensive external consultants signals capability gaps and structural cost pressures
findings.figures: Planning overspend as part of £714k total service-level overspend
findings.quote: Planning is forecasting an overspend as a result of using consultants for planning appeals.  The council does not have the expertise to do this work in house.

findings.headline: Investment income outperformance of £899k entirely masks £714k service-level overspend, creating dependency on high interest rates
findings.detail: The council is forecasting £7.2m investment income against budget of £6.2m. Treasury deposits returned 4.56% versus SONIA benchmark of 3.74%. Without this £899k outperformance, the financial position would show a £715k overspend rather than a £184k underspend. The council holds £55m of investments but achieved interest only from a high-rate environment.
findings.matters: The council's positive reported position relies almost entirely on exceptional investment returns from a temporarily high interest rate environment. If and when rates fall, the underlying operational overspend becomes the actual problem
findings.figures: £899,000 additional investment income forecast; treasury deposit returns 4.56% versus 3.74% SONIA benchmark
findings.quote: The projected full year overspend at service level is forecast to be £714,000, and treasury income to be achieved in year is anticipated to be above budget by £899,000 leading to an overall net underspend of £184,000 at year end.

findings.headline: External quality assessment of internal audit function has not been completed, creating a regulatory compliance gap
findings.detail: The Global Internal Audit Standards (GIAS) require an external assessment of internal audit at least every five years. This requirement has not been met and was only added to the Quality Assurance and Improvement Programme (QAIP) during 2025/26. This means the audit function itself has not been independently verified for compliance or effectiveness.
findings.matters: Without independent external verification, there is reduced assurance that the internal audit function is itself operating effectively and providing reliable oversight of controls.
findings.figures: External assessment requirement: every 5 years; no assessment completed in last 5+ years
findings.quote: It is a requirement of the standards for an external assessment of internal audit to be completed at least every five years. An external assessment has not been undertaken within the last five years and has been added to the QAIP, which is regularly presented to JAGC for review.

findings.headline: Resource constraints within the internal audit team caused the council to miss one of three performance targets and left five audits incomplete as of end of June
findings.detail: The council achieved only 2 of 3 performance targets in 2025/26. Performance Target 3 (completing fieldwork on 80% of operational audits) was achieved at only 74%, with five operational audits still in progress on 26 June. The report attributes delays to 'audits taking longer than budgeted, the need to await the completion of an internal investigation before finalising one audit and resource constraints within the team'.
findings.matters: Under-resourced audit function means the council may not be identifying all control weaknesses or risk areas, reducing the comprehensiveness of the control environment assessment.
findings.figures: 2 of 3 performance targets met; 5 operational audits in progress; PT3 achieved at 74% vs 80% target
findings.quote: The reasons for the delay in completing these audits include audits taking longer than budgeted, the need to await the completion of an internal investigation before finalising one audit and resource constraints within the team.

findings.headline: Four Limited assurance audits in 2025/26, an increase from prior years, concentrated on three residential property facilities with 153 combined management actions
findings.detail: Limited assurance is assigned when 'significant gaps, weaknesses or non-compliance were identified'. Three site visit audits—Abbey House (51 actions), Beacon (50 actions), and Cornerstone (52 actions)—each received Limited ratings. A fourth Limited rating was assigned to Travel & Expenses (9 actions). This represents an uptick: 2024/25 had 2 Limited audits, 2023/24 had 1, and 2022/23 had 2.
findings.matters: The concentration of Limited ratings on residential properties suggests significant control weaknesses in asset management and landlord functions, with material remediation required across three facilities.
findings.figures: 4 Limited audits in 2025/26 vs 2 in 2024/25; Abbey House 51 actions, Beacon 50 actions, Cornerstone 52 actions (153 combined)
findings.quote: Of the 22 completed audits in 2025/26, there were four audits with a Limited assurance rating.

findings.headline: 71 overdue management actions, including 8 Priority 1 findings, indicate control weaknesses are not being remedied promptly
findings.detail: As of 26 June 2026, 117 management actions remain open from audits issued across multiple years. Of these, 71 are overdue, including 8 Priority 1 actions which are described as 'fundamental to the integrity of the service's business processes and require the immediate attention of management'. The report explicitly notes 'further improvement is required to reduce the number of overdue actions and to ensure timely completion'.
findings.matters: Overdue remediation of audit findings indicates the council is not implementing control improvements at pace, suggesting a weaker control environment than the overall satisfactory opinion implies, with key issues unresolved.
findings.figures: 71 overdue actions of 117 open; 8 Priority 1 overdue; 48 Priority 2 overdue; 15 Priority 3 overdue; 212 actions issued in 2025/26 alone
findings.quote: Overall, management is making progress in implementing open actions to address the risks and control weaknesses identified by internal audit. However, further improvement is required to reduce the number of overdue actions and to ensure timely completion.

findings.headline: Capital programme shows £19.3m underspend (58% of budget), indicating project delivery risks
findings.detail: By month nine, the council has only spent £13.9m against an approved capital budget of £33.2m. Major projects are being delayed into 2026/27, including Vehicle Depot (completion now expected 2026/27), Cornerstone decarbonisation (moved from summer 2025 to summer 2026), and affordable housing purchases. The Cornerstone decarbonisation project delay is particularly significant as it was expected to generate substantial cost savings from reduced running costs.
findings.matters: Significant capital programme underspend suggests either unrealistic budgeting or project delivery issues, both indicating execution risk and delayed benefits.
findings.figures: £13.9m spent of £33.2m approved budget by month 9; £19.3m variance; Cornerstone decarbonisation delayed from summer 2025 to summer 2026
findings.quote: Spend is £13.9 million against the approved budget of £33.2 million, therefore showing a variance of £19.3 million.

findings.headline: Recycling budget error resulted in £180,000 overspend
findings.detail: The council identified an error in how the recycling budget was set for 2025/26, causing a £180,000 overspend. Additionally, reduced recycling volumes have resulted in £75,000 less income from county council recycling credits. The council states the error has been resolved for 2026/27.
findings.matters: Budget errors indicate control weaknesses in the finance function and raise questions about the quality of budget scrutiny and preparation processes.
findings.figures: £180,000 overspend from budget error; £75,000 additional overspend from volume reduction
findings.quote: There was an error in setting the recycling budget and as a result, this will be £180,000 overspent.

findings.headline: Council budgeted for 3% vacancy rate that is not materializing, driving £803,000 employee cost overspend
findings.detail: The 2025/26 budget assumed a vacancy factor of less than 3% but actual vacancy levels are much lower, requiring the council to employ or cover work through agency staff. This structural mismatch is contributing to an £803,000 overspend on employee costs. The council is proposing to reduce this contingency in 2026/27, acknowledging the assumption was incorrect.
findings.matters: Fundamental budget assumptions that don't match reality indicate weak financial control and forecast reliability.
findings.figures: £803,000 employee cost overspend; vacancy factor assumption less than three per cent
findings.quote: The 2025/26 budget does not fully fund all staff costs but assumes a vacancy factor of less than three per cent, which is not being met in year

findings.headline: Ocella system replacement project is overrunning with costs higher than originally expected
findings.detail: The Ocella replacement project, which includes software migration and system implementation, is generating cost overruns across multiple departments. In Planning, additional agency staff and increased work scope are required due to the project. In Corporate Services, one-off transformation costs are being incurred for the software migration.
findings.matters: Uncontrolled project costs indicate delivery risks and management capability issues that could affect other council operations and financial stability.
findings.figures: Employee cost overspend in Planning includes agency staff for Ocella work; Corporate Services has one-off transformation costs incurred in IT
findings.quote: This project is overrunning and therefore these additional costs are higher than originally expected.

findings.paper_title: Draft LG Auditor's Annual Report 2024-25 SODC
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation announced December 2024 with this council ceasing to exist after 2027/28
findings.detail: The government's Local Government Reorganisation announcement in December 2024 creates a significant new strategic challenge. The council has submitted a proposal to merge with Vale of White Horse and West Berkshire as a new unitary council ('Ridgeway'). Under the government's timetable, South Oxfordshire District Council will cease to exist after 2027/28, meaning the 4-year medium-term financial plan only covers 3 years of the council's remaining life.
findings.matters: LGR creates material uncertainty for lenders: the council's strategy and financial assumptions may change, integration risks are substantial, and management resources will be diverted to reorganization work. The truncated life of the council affects the validity of medium-term financial planning and the ability to deliver long-term infrastructure investment.
findings.figures: Council ceases after 2027/28
findings.quote: under the government's timetable for Local Government Reorganisation, this council will cease to exist after 2027/28.

findings.paper_title: Draft LG Auditor's Annual Report 2024-25 SODC
findings.headline: Capital programme 46% underspent in 2024/25 with major delivery delays: £6.8m Development and Corporate Landlord, £3.8m Didcot Northern Perimeter Road, £2m Healthcare CIL
findings.detail: Capital expenditure was £18.8m against a working budget of £34.5m, a variance of £15.7m (46% underspend). This was largely due to slippage on major projects: £6.8m on Development and Corporate Landlord (affordable housing and leisure), £3.8m on Didcot Northern Perimeter Road, £2.0m on Community Infrastructure Levy Healthcare payment, and £1.2m on Disabled Facilities Grant. Of this underspend, £15.1m was carried forward to 2025/26.
findings.matters: Sustained capital slippage indicates project delivery capability issues and means planned housing, infrastructure and community facilities are delayed. This affects the council's ability to meet housing growth targets and impacts economic development. Large carried-forward commitments risk similar slippage in 2025/26.
findings.figures: £18.8m spent of £34.5m budget; £15.7m variance; £6.8m landlord, £3.8m Didcot road
