This was largely due to slippage on major projects: • £6.8 million on Development and Corporate Landlord (including Affordable Housing projects and leisure schemes), • £3.8 million on Policy and Programmes (mainly Didcot Northern Perimeter Road)

findings.paper_title: Draft LG Auditor's Annual Report 2024-25 SODC
findings.headline: Service expenditure overbudget by £0.2m, masked entirely by £2.2m excess investment income from elevated interest rates
findings.detail: Service expenditure was £24.7m against a working budget of £24.5m, creating an adverse variance of £0.2m. This overspend was offset entirely by treasury investments generating £8.9m, exceeding budget by £2.2m due to the council placing deposits at interest rates above forecast (driven by increases in the UK bank base rate). The overall result appears positive only because of investment income; underlying service spending is overrunning.
findings.matters: The council's apparent financial position depends on a favorable interest rate environment. If rates decline, the service spending overspend becomes visible and the reserve drawdown accelerates. The base budget is not sustainable at current interest rate assumptions.
findings.figures: £0.2m service overspend, £2.2m excess investment income
findings.quote: The Council reported service expenditure for the year as £24.7 million against a working budget of £24.5 million – equating to an adverse variance of £0.2 million at direct service expenditure level. This was offset by treasury management investment income – Treasury Investments generated £8.9 million, exceeding the budget by £2.2 million.

findings.paper_title: Draft LG Auditor's Annual Report 2024-25 SODC
findings.headline: Revenue expenditure forecast to exceed income from 2025/26 onwards, requiring draw-down of reserves from £38.1m to £23.8m by 2029/30
findings.detail: The chief financial officer's budget robustness report highlights that from 2025/26 onwards, revenue expenditure is expected to exceed income, requiring increased use of reserves over the 4-year medium-term plan. General fund balances and unallocated earmarked reserves will decrease from £38.1m in 2025/26 to £23.8m in 2029/30. The auditor notes this structural deficit underlines the need for a formal savings plan, which has been an outstanding recommendation from the prior year.
findings.matters: A council with falling reserves and a structural deficit will eventually run out of money unless it increases income, reduces spending, or restructures services. This creates medium-term solvency risk and indicates the council is not in surplus. At current trajectory, reserves will be substantially depleted in 4 years.
findings.figures: £38.1m reserves 2025/26 declining to £23.8m by 2029/30; revenue deficit from 2025/26
findings.quote: from 2025/26 onwards, revenue expenditure is expected to exceed income, requiring increased use of reserves.

findings.paper_title: Draft LG Auditor's Annual Report 2024-25 SODC
findings.headline: Red-rated governance weakness: 175 outstanding internal audit recommendations as of September 2025, including 21 high-priority items
findings.detail: The auditor has identified a significant weakness in the council's governance arrangements due to the high number of unresolved internal audit recommendations. As of 5 September 2025, there were 175 actions outstanding, of which 21 were priority 1 (requiring immediate attention of management). Critically, 77 of these actions had been raised in prior years and remain unresolved. This has been an ongoing issue raised in the prior audit, and the council has not resolved it.
findings.matters: Unresolved audit recommendations indicate control failures that have not been remedied. A lender needs to understand whether the council's management is capable of addressing identified control weaknesses. The auditor's assessment of this as a 'significant weakness' is the most serious finding in the report.
findings.figures: 175 actions outstanding, 21 priority 1, 77 raised prior to 2024/25
findings.quote: our view is that this represents a significant weakness in the Council's governance arrangements that the Council should aim to resolve as soon as possible.

findings.headline: Contractor management strategy shifted to extensions rather than renewals due to LGR uncertainty
findings.detail: Multiple third-party contracts are maturing within a similar timeframe. Rather than proceeding with competitive renewal, the council is deliberately extending existing contracts with current providers to reduce operational disruption in light of LGR proposals. This approach postpones competitive procurement decisions.
findings.matters: Lenders need visibility of procurement strategy and supplier relationships. Extending contracts rather than renewing them may defer competition, lock in existing terms, and could indicate that operational decisions are being driven by external uncertainty rather than value-for-money assessment.
findings.figures: none
findings.quote: In light of Local Government Reorganisation some programmes are working towards a contract extension with the current provider rather than being renewed. This action reduces the overall impact on the council.

findings.headline: Four-year balanced budget agreed but future sustainability contingent on outcome of fair funding review still underway
findings.detail: A four-year balanced budget was approved by Council in February 2025. However, the council is explicitly awaiting the outcome of a fair funding review that is currently underway, and this outcome is needed in time for next year's budget setting. The budget's sustainability beyond the initial four years is not yet assured.
findings.matters: A lender needs confidence in sustained budget balance. The explicit dependency on a fair funding review outcome — which will only be known at an unspecified future date — means the council's medium-term financial plan cannot be considered fully resolved.
findings.figures: Four-year balanced budget agreed Feb 2025
findings.quote: A four-year balanced budget has been agreed and approved by Council in Feb 2025... Await outcome of fair funding review now underway in time for next year's budget setting.

findings.headline: Strategic governance work has been delayed because of Local Government Reorganisation uncertainty
findings.detail: The council acknowledges that assessment of its Risk Maturity and definition of Risk Appetite have both been delayed due to LGR proposals. This means the council lacks current formal assessment of its risk profile and risk tolerance against a backdrop of significant structural change.
findings.matters: A lender assessing financial stability needs confidence in a council's understanding of its own risks and risk management capacity. Delay in formalising this assessment signals that strategic planning is paused, and the council's risk profile may be unclear.
findings.figures: none
findings.quote: Work has been delayed in assessing the council's Risk Maturity and defining the councils Risk Appetite due to the proposed Local Government Reorganisation.

findings.headline: Supporting documentation missing for £645k of capital grant receipts in advance; bank reconciliation of £886k not completed
findings.detail: Auditors could not obtain supporting evidence for £645k of capital grant receipts in advance (two transactions above the audit reporting threshold). One bank reconciliation for £886k was not fully reconciled at audit, just containing a list of trial balance transactions. Two other bank reconciliations were dated September rather than year-end.
findings.matters: Missing documentation and unresolved bank reconciliations suggest weak financial controls and record-keeping. At this scale, they indicate either poor process discipline or resource shortage.
findings.figures: £645k with no supporting evidence; £886k unresolved bank reconciliation
findings.quote: Within our testing of Capital Grant receipts in Advance, we identified that there were two amounts (totalling £645k) for which management were unable to produce any evidence. Whilst we were able to conclude that there was no risk of material misstatement, these are transactions which are above our reporting threshold, and for which we would have expected evidence to be available for.

findings.headline: Audit fees increased by £35,617 (23% above £156,634 scale fee) due to prior-year control issues and working paper deficiencies
findings.detail: The scale fee was £156,634. Additional fees totalled £35,617 covering: IFRS 16 implementation (£4,982), rebuilding assurance work (£11,626), working paper issues (£7,740), rework on initial accounts (£2,964), VFM procedures (£3,612), Property, Plant and Equipment (£2,430), pension disclosures (£2,263). The largest cost is rebuilding assurance (£11,626) due to prior-year disclaimers; the second is working paper issues (£7,740).
findings.matters: Fee increases reflect inefficiency and control failures. Lenders should factor in that annual audit costs will remain elevated until the disclaimed opinion is cleared (planned 2026-27), and that internal finance processes need investment.
findings.figures: Scale fee £156,634; total fee £192,251; overrun £35,617 (23%)
findings.quote: Fee variation 2 – Additional procedures to rebuild assurance (Phase 1 as per Section 7 of this report) TBC 11,626; Fee variation 3 – Additional time required to address issues with regards to the supporting working papers, including follow-up queries and following-up on evidence. This is set out in more detail in Section 6. N/A 7,740

findings.headline: Material audit adjustments required including pension recognition error and £14.58m lease receivables disclosure understatement
findings.detail: Auditors required multiple material adjustments: (1) £24.474m pension remeasurement because a pension asset was incorrectly recognised as an asset rather than a liability in breach of IFRIC 14; (2) £14.58m understatement of net investment in finance leases in Note 22 (with similar £14.656m error in prior year); (3) £3.91m classification error in Employee Benefits Expenses. These are adjusted items, meaning they were corrected, but signal control gaps in account preparation.
findings.matters: Large adjustments show the accounts as originally prepared were materially misstated. Repeated similar errors (£14.58m lease error in both current and prior year) show systemic process failures, not one-off mistakes.
findings.figures: £24.474m pension remeasurement; £14.58m lease receivables understatement; £3.91m payroll classification; total adjustments £24.606m income statement, £28.570m balance sheet
findings.quote: Our work identified material misstatements with regard to the recognition of a pension asset, which should have been a liability in compliance with IFRIC 14. This has been amended.

findings.headline: Unaudited accounts delivered late and then revised, requiring auditors to redo work and causing unexplained delays
findings.detail: The council submitted unaudited accounts on 10 July 2025, 10 days after the 30 June statutory deadline. These were then revised and resubmitted on 26 August 2025, forcing auditors to redo checks including 'initial review by the Key Audit Partner and Manager as well as some basic casting and comparative reviews.' The reason for the revision is not given in the management comment.
findings.matters: Late accounts delay audit, increase audit costs (fees up £35k for additional work), and suggest internal control or resource issues. The unexplained restatement raises questions about quality of preparation and whether numbers were final.
findings.figures: 10 July 2025 submission (10 days late); 26 August 2025 revision; additional audit fees £35,617
findings.quote: We were provided with a copy of the unaudited financial statements on 10 July 2025, after the statutory deadline of 30 June. However these were subsequently revised, and a second version was provided to us on 26 August 2025.

findings.headline: Council identified significant governance weakness in failure to implement or progress internal audit recommendations
findings.detail: The auditors identified 'a significant weakness in the Council's governance arrangements for the year ended 31 March 2025, in relation to the failure to implement or achieve progress on recommendations raised by Internal Audit.' This is a Value for Money finding, not a routine point. It indicates management is not acting on identified control weaknesses.
findings.matters: Failure to implement audit recommendations is a governance red flag that signals either weak leadership or resource constraints. It suggests control weaknesses are known but not being fixed, which undermines the entire control environment.
findings.figures: One significant governance weakness identified
findings.quote: Our Value for Money work identified a significant weakness in the Council's governance arrangements for the year ended 31 March 2025, in relation to the failure to implement or achieve progress on recommendations raised by Internal Audit.

findings.headline: Audit opinion will be disclaimed for the second consecutive year due to inability to assure opening balances
findings.detail: The council will receive a disclaimed opinion for 2024-25, following a disclaimed opinion in 2023-24 and 2022-23 when the previous auditor did no substantive work. The auditors plan to rebuild assurance over three years, targeting an unqualified opinion in 2026-27. The lack of opening balance assurance cascades from the prior-year disclaimers.
findings.matters: Disclaimed opinions prevent lenders from having any audit-backed confidence in the council's reported financial position. Two consecutive disclaimers signal systemic audit failure, not a one-off problem.
findings.figures: 2023-24 disclaimed; 2024-25 disclaimed (planned); 2025-26 qualified (planned); 2026-27 unqualified (target)
findings.quote: Subject to the satisfactory finalisation of these points, we anticipate issuing a modified disclaimed opinion. This is due to the lack of assurance over opening balances in 2024/25, resulting from the opinions on both the 2022/23 and 2023/24 financial statements being disclaimed.

findings.paper_title: Revenue budget 2026/27 and capital programme 2026/27 to 2030/31, 05/02/2026 Cabinet
findings.headline: Capital receipts will be nearly depleted by 2030/31, limiting capital flexibility
findings.detail: Usable capital receipts are forecast to fall to just £1.385m by 31 March 2031. This sharply reduces the council's ability to fund emergency repairs, adapt to changing priorities, or respond to unexpected capital needs without seeking external grants, developer contributions (S106/CIL), or prudential borrowing.
findings.matters: The council will have minimal capital reserves to fund repairs or respond to capital emergencies, forcing reliance on borrowing at a time when revenue budgets are under severe stress.
findings.figures: £1,385,000 usable capital receipts estimated to remain by 31 March 2031
findings.quote: The council's usable capital receipts, based on current estimates, are expected to be £1.385 million by the end of 2030/31.

findings.paper_title: Revenue budget 2026/27 and capital programme 2026/27 to 2030/31, 05/02/2026 Cabinet
findings.headline: £15m loan to South Oxfordshire Housing Association represents significant concentration risk
findings.detail: The council has an ongoing £15m loan to South Oxfordshire Housing Association, which forms part of its £35m permitted capital investment portfolio. This loan is not capable of being realised quickly and represents the council's largest single asset investment. A financial distress event at SOHA could materially impair the council's balance sheet.
findings.matters: Default by a single investee could materially impair the council's financial position and reduce available resources to manage other budget pressures.
findings.figures: £15,000,000 ongoing loan to SOHA; embedded in £35,000,000 total permitted capital investment portfolio
findings.quote: As at 31 March 2030 the council is currently projected to have invested or earmarked the £35 million permitted in capital schemes, including an ongoing £15 million loan to South Oxfordshire Housing Association.

findings.paper_title: Revenue budget 2026/27 and capital programme 2026/27 to 2030/31, 05/02/2026 Cabinet
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation timeline is unconfirmed; any delay breaks the budget model
findings.detail: The council is planning for Local Government Reorganisation (LGR) from April 2028, at which point it expects to cease to exist. However, this timeline is not confirmed. The budget notes that if LGR is delayed, the MTFP demonstrates increasing reliance on reserve drawdown in later years — precisely the point where the council's reserves are already becoming unsustainable.
findings.matters: If LGR is delayed beyond 2028/29, the council will face a severe financial crisis with no path to a balanced budget and insufficient reserves.
findings.figures: £3,000,000 set aside for LGR costs; planned council supersession from 1 April 2028
findings.quote: The ultimate timeline for LGR will also be a factor as, should LGR be delayed, the MTFP demonstrates an increasing reliance on the use of reserves in later years.

findings.paper_title: Revenue budget 2026/27 and capital programme 2026/27 to 2030/31, 05/02/2026 Cabinet
findings.headline: Transitional protection of £112k will expire in 2029/30, triggering real-terms funding cuts
findings.detail: The council is receiving transitional protection of £112,917 because it is on the government's funding floor. This protection is expected to last only three years (through 2028/29). From 2029/30 onwards, the council will receive only inflationary increases to its fair funding allocation, meaning real-terms reductions in government funding.
findings.matters: The council faces real-terms funding cuts from 2029/30 onwards, just as its capacity to absorb these through reserve depletion is exhausted.
findings.figures: £112,917 transitional protection in 2026/27; protection expected to last 3 years (through end of 2028/29)
findings.quote: For 2029/30 and 2030/31, the fair funding allocation amounts shown above continue to be increased by inflation but without the transitional protection as this is expected to last for three years only.

findings.paper_title: Revenue budget 2026/27 and capital programme 2026/27 to 2030/31, 05/02/2026 Cabinet
findings.headline: Council forecasts £6.3m investment returns for 2026/27; £5m to support future budgets, £616k current-year expenditure
findings.detail: The council forecasts £6.3m of investment returns in 2026/27. Of this, £5m is being transferred to reserves to support future budgets and £616k is supporting current-year expenditure. If interest rates fall from current levels, this income will decline sharply, opening a material budget gap.
findings.matters: A fall in interest rates would create a significant funding shortfall in both current and future budgets, forcing additional reserve drawdown or service reductions at the point where reserves are becoming critical.
findings.figures: £6,296,208 total forecast investment returns; £5,000,000 transferred to support future budgets; £616,208 supporting current-year expenditure
findings.quote: Investment returns for 2026/27 are currently forecast to be £6,296,208 and will be allocated as follows: £5,000,000 to support future revenue budgets, £616,208 to support in-year revenue expenditure, £320,000 to fund capital expenditure on community grants scheme, £360,000 reinvested in financial instruments.

findings.paper_title: Revenue budget 2026/27 and capital programme 2026/27 to 2030/31, 05/02/2026 Cabinet
findings.headline: Internal borrowing will create revenue budget pressure from 2027/28 onwards
findings.detail: Rather than borrowing externally, the council is using its cash balances to fund capital expenditure (internal borrowing). This will require revenue budgets to include Minimum Revenue Provision (MRP) repayments starting in 2027/28. The council forecasts requiring approximately £170,000 for MRP in 2027/28, with further commitments in subsequent years.
findings.matters: Future revenue budgets will face growing debt service costs that reduce financial flexibility and compound the reserve depletion problem.
findings.figures: £170,000 MRP forecast for 2027/28
findings.quote: the council will need to make a provision in the revenue budget in future years for the principal amount of the internal borrowing it has undertaken. This is expected to be in the region of £170,000 in 2027/28.

findings.paper_title: Revenue budget 2026/27 and capital programme 2026/27 to 2030/31, 05/02/2026 Cabinet
findings.headline: Council becomes unable to balance budgets without reserves after 2028/29
findings.detail: The Medium-Term Financial Plan shows the council will need to draw reserves to balance budgets from 2028/29 onwards. However, the plan explicitly states this cannot continue 'beyond that financial year' within sustainability parameters. This creates a structural budget gap just as the council approaches the planned Local Government Reorganisation date.
findings.matters: Lenders need to know the council cannot sustain balanced budgets beyond 2028/29 without major service reductions or external intervention.
findings.figures: None specified for the shortfall amount, but extends across 2028/29 to 2030/31 forecast period
findings.quote: From 2028/29 onwards the council is projected to use reserves to balance its budget. This it can do within the sustainability parameters in 2028/29, but not beyond that financial year.

findings.headline: Five-year capital programme of £102.8m funded by £14m prudential borrowing alongside grants and developer contributions
findings.detail: The capital programme totals £102.8m (2025/26–2030/31), financed by grants (£23.1m), developer contributions S106 and CIL (£42.4m), capital receipts (£20.9m), and borrowing of £13.5m (stated as £14m in section 11.5). Revenue financing costs are included in the budget.
findings.matters: The borrowing level is material relative to a likely annual council revenue budget. This commits future revenue budgets to debt service and signals capital-intensive strategy affecting financial flexibility.
findings.figures: Total programme £102,789k. Borrowing £13,500k approved (£14m stated in text). External funding: grants £23,128k, S106 £15,654k, CIL £26,715k.
findings.quote: The council's current capital programme includes borrowing of £14 million to finance capital expenditure. The revenue implications of debt financing costs are included in the council's revenue budget.

findings.headline: Council proposes local government reorganisation merging with Vale of White Horse and West Berkshire as single unitary authority
findings.detail: In November 2025 the council agreed to submit a proposal for a new unitary council covering South Oxfordshire, Vale of White Horse, and West Berkshire. The capital programme development has considered the impact of this structural change, though specific financial implications are not detailed.
findings.matters: A major structural change affecting governance, service delivery model, and financial arrangements. Creates material uncertainty about future costs, service efficiency, and the council's financial position as a unitary authority.
findings.figures: Proposal covers three existing councils; decision made November 2025
findings.quote: In November 2025 the council agreed to submit a proposal for a new unitary council covering the existing boundaries of South Oxfordshire, the Vale of White Horse and West Berkshire District Councils.

findings.headline: Usable capital receipts will fall to £1.174m by 2031 as five-year programme depletes this finite resource
findings.detail: The capital programme table projects usable capital receipts declining to £1.174m by March 2031. This represents significant depletion of a key one-time funding source across a £102.8m capital spending plan. Future programmes will depend more heavily on borrowing or grants unless the council's asset disposal strategy succeeds.
findings.matters: Capital receipts are a finite reserve. Heavy depletion signals that the council's future capital flexibility will be constrained unless asset disposals materialise as planned, potentially forcing greater reliance on borrowing or service cuts.
findings.figures: Estimated usable capital receipts as at 31 March 2031: £1,174k (down from current balances after spending £20,899k across the programme)
findings.quote: Estimated balances as at 31 March 2031 Usable capital receipts 1,174

findings.headline: Council commits £10m to acquire approximately 30 homes for temporary and general needs housing
findings.detail: In July 2025 the council approved a further £10m of capital investment to purchase approximately 30 homes for temporary or general needs housing under its housing delivery strategy. This is a material capital commitment with revenue implications—running costs, maintenance, and potential subsidy or rental income—that are not detailed in this strategy document.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand not just the capital outlay but the ongoing revenue cost of operating council housing stock. The council's revenue budget impact from this £10m housing commitment is not disclosed here.
findings.figures: £10m capital commitment for approximately 30 homes; decision made July 2025
findings.quote: In July 2025 the council agreed to invest a further £10m of its capital funds to purchase approximately 30 homes for use as temporary or general needs housing.

findings.paper_title: South s151 report on adequacy and robustness Feb 2026
findings.headline: LGR reorganisation timeline is uncertain and may prevent necessary long-term cost reductions, worsening the reserve sustainability position.
findings.detail: The council is expected to be abolished and replaced by unitary authorities from April 2028, but this timeline is not fixed. The s151 report explicitly states that 'should LGR be delayed, the MTFP demonstrates an increasing reliance on the use of reserves in later years'. The council has set aside £3m for transition costs, adding financial drag.
findings.matters: Uncertainty about the council's end date creates a perverse incentive not to implement unpopular cost reductions; if reorganisation is delayed, the council becomes locked into unsustainable reserve drawdown.
findings.figures: £3m set aside for LGR transition; expected April 2028 but timeline uncertain
findings.quote: The ultimate timeline for LGR will also be a factor as, should LGR be delayed, the MTFP demonstrates an increasing reliance on the use of reserves in later years.

findings.paper_title: South s151 report on adequacy and robustness Feb 2026
findings.headline: Assumed staff vacancy savings of £500k were never achieved due to high retention; reduced to £250k for 2026/27 but flagged for continued review, signalling budget planning risk.
findings.detail: The council has historically assumed £500k annual savings from staff vacancies, but high retention rates meant these were never delivered. These shortfalls were covered by other savings, masking the structural overspend. The council has reduced the assumption to £250k but admits this 'will be kept under review', implying uncertainty about whether even this target is achievable.
findings.matters: A persistent miss on efficiency targets suggests future staff-cost budgets may also be optimistic, creating a pattern of recurring overspends that must be absorbed elsewhere.
findings.figures: £500,000 historical assumption; reduced to £250,000 for 2026/27
findings.quote: in previous years the budget assumed a level of expected vacancy savings of £500,000. Over recent years, the high level of staff retention across the council has meant that this assumed vacancy level has not been achieved, and the resulting overspend has been able to be covered by savings or increased income across the council. For 2026/27 the level of expected savings had been reduced to £250,000 and will be kept under review for future budgets.

findings.paper_title: South s151 report on adequacy and robustness Feb 2026
findings.headline: Material sensitivity to interest rate falls on £6.3m investment income that supports the operating budget; a 0.5% rate change swings income by £750k.
findings.detail: The council budgets £6.3m investment income as a core component of its 2026/27 revenue budget. Interest rates have been volatile—reaching 5.25% in 2023, falling to 3.75% in December 2025. The council estimates that a 0.5% variance in returns creates a £750k variance in income.
findings.matters: If interest rates fall further, the council could face unexpected budget shortfalls of £750k or more with very short notice, forcing emergency cuts or reserves draw.
findings.figures: £6.3 million investment income; 0.5% rate variance = £750,000 income impact
findings.quote: Whilst the budget for 2026/27 shows that £6.3 million of income will be earned in year, most of that income is not committed until the year after it is earned, providing certainty about the amount available when the budgets are set. As context, if the estimated rate of return for 2026/27 was 0.5 per cent higher or lower than the actual rate of return, then the financial impact of that is estimated to be a variation of £750,000 in income received.

findings.paper_title: South s151 report on adequacy and robustness Feb 2026
findings.headline: Structural funding cliff when the 'funding floor' ends in 2028/29, causing core spending power to fall after three years of frozen grants.
findings.detail: The council is protected by a three-year funding floor (2026/27 to 2028/29) guaranteeing static core spending power. However, the settlement is explicit that funding 'is expected to fall after 2028/29 as the transitional protection ends'. Revenue Support Grant will decline while council tax increases are limited by referendum thresholds.
findings.matters: The timing of this funding cliff (2028/29) coincides exactly with the start of unsustainable reserve draws, creating a structural double squeeze on the council's finances.
findings.figures: Three-year static funding floor 2026/27-2028/29; expected fall thereafter
findings.quote: The combined value of council tax, Revenue Support Grant (RSG) and transitional protection income will remain static during that three year period but is expected to fall after 2028/29 as the transitional protection ends.

findings.paper_title: South s151 report on adequacy and robustness Feb 2026
findings.headline: Council tax base is constrained at 46% below average for shire districts, eliminating tax-raising flexibility to address budget shortfalls.
findings.detail: South Oxfordshire's Band D council tax of £151.24 is the 10th lowest nationally among shire districts, compared to a £221.24 average. This £70-per-property gap represents 46% below peer average and cannot be easily closed due to reputational and political constraints.
findings.matters: Low tax base means the council cannot use council tax increases as a lever to balance budgets when central funding falls or demand pressures rise, reducing financial resilience.
findings.figures: Band D: £151.24 vs shire district average £221.24; 10th lowest nationally; £70 per property gap; 46% below average
findings.quote: In 2025/26, its Band D council tax level of £151.24 per annum was the 10th lowest in the country for shire districts. The average for shire districts was £221.24 per annum – a gap of £70 per property or 46 per cent.

findings.paper_title: South s151 report on adequacy and robustness Feb 2026
findings.headline: Reserves draw of £3.4m in 2029/30 reaches 9% of available reserves, approaching council's 10% sustainability limit
findings.detail: The MTFP shows the council running surpluses in 2026/27 and 2027/28, but from 2028/29 revenue expenditure exceeds income, requiring increasing draws on reserves. The 2029/30 draw of £3.4m is flagged as 'much closer to the limit of sustainability' at 9%, and the council states that usage beyond the MTFP period would be 'unsustainable'. The council has set a 10% annual usage limit as its sustainability threshold.
findings.matters: A council drawing down reserves at or near its stated sustainability limit signals it cannot balance operations through normal revenue means; this is a critical risk metric for lenders.
findings.figures: £3.4 million draw in 2029/30; 9% of available reserves; 10% annual limit stated as unsustainable threshold
findings.quote: The projected use of reserves in 2029/30 is a significant sum - £3.4 million – and is much closer to the limit of sustainability at nine per cent. The use of reserves in the final year of the MTFP and beyond would be unsustainable.

findings.paper_title: Treasury management and investment strategy 2026/27, 05/02/2026 Cabinet
findings.headline: Council is moving to internal borrowing for the first time, creating a Minimum Revenue Provision liability of £330,000 annually.
findings.detail: South Oxfordshire has no current external debt but is now required to use internal borrowing to finance capital expenditure. This creates a structural revenue cost: £330,000 for MRP (principal repayment) and £970,200 for interest annually on an assumed £16.5 million borrowing. The capital financing requirement is forecast to reach £16.5 million by 2030/31.
findings.matters: A lender would need to understand the council's shift from a debt-free position and assess its capacity to service £1.3 million annual debt charges. The finance director needs to track this new structural commitment.

The Head of Finance will determine the most appropriate repayment method, term of borrowing and duration of borrowing. The Capital Financing Requirement (CFR) estimate for the council is £16.5 million by the end of 2030/31.

news_drafts.headline: South Oxfordshire: 67 of 131 open internal audit actions past deadline, including eight Priority 1
news_drafts.lead:
South Oxfordshire's Joint Audit and Governance Committee has been told that 67 of the 131 open actions from internal audit, the council's in-house check on whether its controls work, were past their deadlines on 25 September 2026. Eight of the 16 open Priority 1 actions, which the auditors define as fundamental to the integrity of a process, are overdue.

The report links the overdue Priority 1 actions to site visit audits at Abbey House, Cornerstone and Beacon. All three were rated Limited assurance. Together they produced 46 of the 87 actions in the 2025/26 audit plan, 19 of them Priority 1. Of the 131 open actions, 96 were raised in 2025/26 and 2026/27. Since the last update, internal audit raised 65 new actions and 105 were closed, while 51 are implemented and awaiting evidence or validation. Audits of cyber security, including artificial intelligence, and of travel and expenses were also rated Limited. The cyber audit raised nine actions, two of them Priority 1. The travel audit raised four, one of them Priority 1.

The papers report better news on other fronts. Neither South Oxfordshire nor Vale of White Horse had any external borrowing at 31 March 2026. South Oxfordshire's authorised limit, the most total debt it has told itself it will not exceed, was set at £35m. A licensing audit rated Substantial assurance, up from Satisfactory when it was last audited in May 2017. It found no discrepancies in fees tested against the 2025-26 schedule and raised only four Priority 3 actions.

Auditors also found some licence changes lacked evidence of compliance with statutory advertising requirements. None of the 39 licensing procedures reviewed had documented review dates, and some had not been reviewed since December 2020. In a separate audit, rated Substantial, five of 20 sampled report checklists (one South Oxfordshire, four Vale) lacked specialist officer sign-off on the implications sections.

news_drafts.headline: South Oxfordshire's budget surplus masks service-level overspend
news_drafts.lead: South Oxfordshire Council forecasts a £184,000 underspend for the year. But the council's own accounts show this surplus is entirely due to higher-than-expected investment income. Services across the council are forecast to overspend by £714,000. The council expects to receive £899,000 more in investment income than budgeted because interest rates have remained elevated. It holds £55m in investments. Without this extra investment income, the council would face a £714,000 overspend. The financial position is therefore dependent on the interest rate environment remaining high.
